ACT I · CARD 03 · NEUROSCIENCE
This Is a Wiring Difference. Not a Behaviour Problem.
What's Happening in the Brain
Somatosensory Cortex: May over- or under-process touch signals — making materials feel alarming, uncomfortable, or invisible.
Cerebellum: May not sequence motor movements efficiently — causing awkward grips, dropped objects, and poor coordination.
Prefrontal Cortex: May struggle to initiate and sustain goal-directed hand movements — so starting tasks feels enormous.
Corpus Callosum: May under-connect the two hemispheres — making bilateral tasks like lacing, cutting, and writing extraordinarily hard.
The Therapeutic Truth
These pathways are not fixed. Structured, repeated sensorimotor input — delivered consistently — physically strengthens neural connections.
Your home session generates 700+ therapeutic repetitions per week versus only 50 in a single clinic session. That difference is everything.

Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020): Repeated structured input drives somatosensory cortex adaptation and cerebellar coordination refinement. DOI:10.3389/fnint.2020.556660

ACT II · CARD 07 · DISCIPLINES
Six Disciplines. One Technique.
Because the brain doesn't organise by therapy type. Every professional on your child's team has a role in the F-619 home programme.
Occupational Therapist (Primary Lead)
Designs material selection and progression sequence. Assesses sensory profile to determine putty resistance grade, sensory bin medium, and cutting progression stage. Provides parent training.
Neuro-Developmental Paediatrician
Establishes neurological baseline and confirms material safety relative to diagnosis, comorbidities, and medication interactions. Validates therapeutic goals against developmental trajectory.
Speech-Language Pathologist
Integrates fine motor activities with language tasks — naming colours while sorting, requesting tools using AAC. Hand-mouth coordination links directly to oral motor development.
ABA / BCBA Therapist
Designs the reinforcement schedule for each material. Builds the motivation ladder — pairing preferred items with therapeutic materials. Uses token economy to sustain engagement.
Special Educator
Bridges home OT practice to academic skill readiness. Scissors → classroom cutting. Pegboards → mathematical patterning. Vertical surfaces → whiteboard writing preparation.
Parent / Primary Caregiver (Home Lead)
The most critical member of this team. With F-619, the parent becomes the delivery system for 700+ therapeutic repetitions per week. Pinnacle GPT-OS provides the data feedback loop.
"This technique crosses therapy boundaries because your child's development is not divided into departments." — Pinnacle Blooms Network Multi-Disciplinary Consortium

ACT II · CARD 09 · PRIMARY MATERIALS
The Complete Home OT Kit. 9 Materials. One Transformation.
Total Kit Investment: Commercial Kit: ₹1,500–5,500 total | DIY Kit: ₹0–800 total. See Card 10 for zero-cost alternatives for every material. Start with 3 materials: Therapy Putty + Tweezers + Sensory Bin. Master these before adding others.
1. Therapy Putty
Hand strength in a pocket-sized package. Squeeze, pull, pinch, and twist to build intrinsic hand muscles. Resistance grades: TAN (XX-Soft) → BLACK (X-Firm). Start with softest resistance. ₹200–600/tub
2. Tweezers and Tongs
Pincer power through picking practice. The same pinch that picks up a pom-pom holds a pencil. Use with pom-poms, dried beans, small blocks. Spring tweezers for ages 2–4. ₹150–400/set
3. Lacing Cards and Beads
Two hands learning to work together. Builds the coordination foundation for cutting, tying, and writing. Bead stringing = sequencing + bilateral coordination combined. ₹250–700/set
4. Sensory Bin
Touch, explore, and regulate. Tactile tolerance meets fine motor practice. Fillings: coloured rice, dried dal, kinetic sand. Add hidden objects for extra OT challenge. ₹300–800
5. Child Safety Scissors
Cutting builds coordination, not just crafts. Every snip strengthens bilateral coordination. Spring-loaded recommended for beginners. Loop scissors for children with grip difficulties. ₹100–350/pair
6. Pegboard
Precision practice, peg by peg. Fingertip precision built peg by peg — feeds directly into pencil grip. Large → medium → small pegs over time. Pattern cards build visual-motor integration. ₹350–900/set
7. Balance Board
Stable core, steady hands. Fine motor control begins with core stability. A wobbly body cannot direct fine movements. Wobble cushion is an excellent lower-cost alternative. ₹800–2,500
8. Vertical Surface Tools
Wrist position and shoulder strength in one setup. Any wall becomes therapy space. Vertical work automatically positions the wrist for writing readiness. ₹0 (wall + tape) to ₹1,500
9. Visual Timer and Schedule
Structure makes practice happen. Time Timer or sand hourglass shows elapsed time visually — reduces "how long?" anxiety. Picture schedule reduces transition resistance. ₹200–800

ACT II · CARD 11 · SAFETY
Safety Is the First Therapeutic Act.
🔴 STOP — Do NOT Proceed If:
  • Child is in active meltdown or severe emotional dysregulation
  • Child has an open wound or active skin condition on hands
  • Child has recently eaten (within 30 minutes) — for putty and sensory bin work
  • Child is showing signs of illness (fever, nausea, extreme fatigue)
  • Small parts present with a child who mouths objects and is under age 3 without direct supervision
  • Child is showing signs of pain, not just discomfort, during any activity
🟡 MODIFY — Proceed with Adaptations If:
  • Child is mildly dysregulated → start with calming material (sensory bin, putty)
  • Child is resistant to a specific material → try DIY version first; reduce to 60 seconds
  • Child is tired → shorten to 5–7 minutes; reduce material count to 2
  • Sibling or other children present → separate space; remove competing stimuli
🟢 PROCEED — All Conditions Met:
  • Child is fed (at least 30 minutes since last meal)
  • Child is rested (not within 30 minutes of sleep)
  • Child is in a calm-alert state (not over-excited or upset)
  • Space is prepared (see Card 12) and materials are within reach

RED LINE — Immediately stop and contact your OT if: increasing distress beyond 3 minutes, self-injurious behaviour, complete material rejection for 3+ consecutive sessions, unusual pain responses, or regression in previously mastered skills. National Autism Helpline: 9100 181 181
ACT II · CARD 12 · SPACE SETUP
The Right Environment Does Half the Work.
Environment Checklist
  • Lighting: Natural light preferred; no flickering fluorescent
  • Sound: Quiet or soft instrumental music; no TV or screen active
  • Temperature: Comfortable — cold hands reduce fine motor performance
  • Distractions removed: Toys not in use stored away
  • Phone silenced — your full attention equals child's best session
  • Small objects secured away from younger siblings
Table Layout (Left to Right)
Putty | Tweezers + Poms | Scissors | Lacing Cards | Pegboard | Visual Timer
Floor area: Sensory bin on low table or floor mat | Balance board on non-slip mat with 1m clearance
17-Minute Session Structure
Setup and transition in: 2 min — Show visual schedule, start timer
Warm-up material (putty or bin): 3 min — Low-demand sensory engagement
Core OT activity 1: 4 min — Tweezers, lacing, or pegboard
Core OT activity 2: 4 min — Scissors or vertical surface
Balance board: 2 min — Parent within arm's reach throughout
Cool-down and data capture: 2 min — Tidy up ritual, praise, quick tick

Sensory Integration Theory (Ayres): Environmental preparation is a core clinical principle. Meta-analysis (PMC10955541) confirms structured 1:1 sessions in prepared environments produce maximum OT outcome effectiveness.

ACT III · CARD 14 · STEP 1: INVITATION
Step 1: The Invitation
Every protocol begins with an invitation, not a command. The child is brought into the activity through playful, low-demand engagement. No: "It's OT time." Yes: "I found something cool — want to see?"
Opening Scripts by Material
Therapy Putty: "Look what I have — it's squishy! Should we see what it does?"
Tweezers + Pom-poms: "I have a little rescue mission. These pom-poms need help getting to their cups. Want to try?"
Sensory Bin: "There's something hidden in here. I wonder what we'll find..."
Scissors: "I need a helper to cut this paper into tiny pieces. Are you the expert?"
Pegboard: "Let's make a pattern. You choose the colours first."
Balance Board: "This is a surfboard. Can you stand on it like a surfer?"
Vertical Surface: "The wall is our art studio today. Big, huge drawing — what should we make?"
Lacing Cards: "This bear needs new shoes. Can you lace them up?"
Acceptance Cues (Child Is Ready)
  • Moves toward the material or reaches for it
  • Makes eye contact or vocalises curiosity
  • Sits or stands near the setup
Resistance Cues (Modify Invitation)
  • Walks away or turns body; pushes material away
  • Vocalises refusal or distress; goes limp
If resistance: Pause. Do not repeat command. Wait 30 seconds. Try again with a different material from the kit.
ACT III · CARD 15 · STEP 2: ENGAGEMENT
Step 2: The Engagement
The child is now engaged. This step deepens the interaction by introducing the therapeutic material properly. The parent follows a precise presentation sequence while reading the child's responses. Reinforcement begins here.
Phase A — SHOW
Hold up the material. Let child look. Name it simply: "This is putty. Red putty."
Phase B — MODEL
Parent interacts with material first. "Watch, I'm squeezing it."
Phase C — OFFER
Place within reach but don't place in child's hands. "Your turn."
Phase D — RESPOND
Whatever the child does first — accept it. Squeeze, drop, poke, smell — all valid first responses.
Child Response Spectrum
Engaged: Child manipulates material purposefully, asks questions, requests more.
Tolerating: Child touches material, stays in seat, allows session to continue. → Reduce material proximity slightly. Reinforce any small interaction.
Avoidant: Child physically moves away, resists, vocalises refusal. → Move to different material immediately. Never force hand contact with sensory material.
Reinforcement Starts Now
Every spontaneous interaction with the material = immediate specific verbal praise.
"Yes! You squeezed it! That was a STRONG squeeze!"
Timing: within 3 seconds of the behaviour.

PMC11506176: Sensory integration intervention with structured material introduction meets evidence-based practice criteria.
ACT III · CARD 16 · STEP 3: THERAPEUTIC ACTION
Step 3: The Therapeutic Action
The main therapeutic event. This is the specific motor pattern or sensory input that constitutes each material's active therapeutic ingredient — described with enough precision to execute correctly and enough flexibility that natural variation is welcomed.
Therapy Putty — Hand Strengthening
Squeeze full-hand 10× → pinch thumb + index 10× → pinch thumb + middle 10× → pull putty apart 5× → hide objects for excavation. Duration: 3–5 min. Common error: Parent helps too much — let the child work the resistance.
Tweezers — Pincer Precision
Pick up pom-poms from flat surface, deposit into muffin tin cups. Start large (pom-poms) → progress to small (dried dal). 10–15 transfers. Duration: 3–4 min. Common error: Offering too-small objects too early.
Lacing Cards — Bilateral Threading
Parent holds card, child threads lace through holes OR child holds card in non-dominant hand. Bead stringing: 5–10 beads per session. Duration: 4–5 min. Common error: Holding the card for child — the non-dominant hand HOLDING is part of the therapy.
Sensory Bin — Tactile Exploration
Free exploration 2 min → add tool 2 min → hide and find objects 2 min. Progression: dry media → damp media → wet media. Duration: 5–6 min. Common error: Rushing past free exploration — the first 2 minutes of tolerance-building is the therapy.
Scissors — 9-Week Cutting Arc
Wk 1–2: Snipping fringe → Wk 3–4: Cutting playdough snakes → Wk 5–6: Cutting straight paper strips → Wk 7–8: Cutting drawn straight line → Wk 9+: Simple curves. Duration: 3–5 min. Common error: Jumping straight to line-cutting.
Pegboard — Pincer + Visual-Motor
Random placement first, then patterned. Introduce colour-pattern cards after 2 weeks of mastery. 20–30 peg placements. Duration: 4–5 min. Common error: Pegs too small for child's current development.
Balance Board — Core Activation
Parent support for first 2 weeks. Count 10 sec → rock forward/back 5× → rock side/side 5× → static hold 15 sec. Duration: 2 min. Common error: Removing adult support too early.
Vertical Surface — Wrist Extension
Paper at eye height. Draw, trace, or copy shapes. Start large (whole-arm movements) → reduce size over weeks. Duration: 3–4 min. Common error: Paper placed too low — the therapeutic benefit requires the arm reaching up and out.
Visual Timer — Practice Compliance
Show visual schedule at session start. Flip/start timer at each activity. Child watches time reduce. "All done" ritual at session end. Used throughout all other activities — not a standalone timed activity.

The Variation Principle
After 3–4 repetitions, introduce a variation within the same motor pattern to maintain engagement while deepening neural pathway formation.
  • Putty: Squeeze → pinch → twist → flatten → hide objects
  • Tweezers: Same objects, different containers → sort by colour → pick from different depths
  • Scissors: Change paper weight → change strip width → change starting position
  • Sensory Bin: Change the filling medium weekly
Satiation Indicators — STOP If You See:
  • Child drops or throws material
  • Child stands up and walks away
  • Child becomes persistently distracted
  • Child vocalises "all done" or equivalent
  • Engagement quality drops significantly
ACT III · CARD 18 · STEP 5: REINFORCE
Step 5: Reinforce and Celebrate
Timing matters more than magnitude. Immediate, specific, enthusiastic reinforcement delivered within 3 seconds of a desired behaviour builds the association: this activity feels good. Celebrate the attempt, not just the success.
Verbal Praise
Immediate, specific, enthusiastic. "Amazing strong squeeze!" Suitable for all children.
Physical Celebration
High five, clap together, fist bump — if the child accepts touch.
Token Economy
Sticker chart — 1 sticker per completed activity. 5 stickers = chosen reward. ABA-integrated.
Natural Consequence
"Because you cut it, we can now make the paper airplane!" Task completion = access to outcome.
Preferred Activity Access
"2 more minutes of bin time because you did so well!" Links reinforcement to the session itself.
Sensory Reward
For sensory seekers — brief swing, bounce, or movement break as reward.

The Rosette Imprint Reward Jar (Pinnacle Canon Product, ₹589) and Reward Sticker Book (₹364) integrate directly with this reinforcement step. Available at Amazon.in. ABA Reinforcement Principles: Immediate, specific reinforcement increases behaviour occurrence.
ACT III · CARD 19 · STEP 6: COOL-DOWN
Step 6: The Cool-Down
No session ends abruptly. The cool-down transitions the child from therapeutic engagement back to baseline — preventing the post-session "crash" that many parents experience after intense OT activity.
Transition Warning (2 min before end)
Verbal and visual cue. Show the visual schedule: last item has a checkmark. "We're almost finished." At 1 minute: "One more. Last one."
Material Put-Away Ritual (1 min)
Child participates in putting materials away if able. "Putty goes back in its pot. Tweezers go in the cup." Builds responsibility + signals transition clearly.
Proprioceptive Calming Input (1–2 min)
If child is over-aroused: deep pressure on shoulders, bear hug if accepted, sit in bean bag, or heavy work task (carry the sensory bin to its spot).
Transition Cue
Name the next activity clearly: "Now it's snack time" or "Now we wash hands." The schedule card shows what comes next.

If child resists ending: Offer "last time" — "One more peg, then we put it away." Never just take the material. Animate the put-away: "Let's rescue all the pom-poms back to their home!" NCAEP (2020): Visual supports and transition warnings are evidence-based practices that reduce post-session dysregulation.

ACT III · CARD 21 · TROUBLESHOOTING
Every Challenge Has a Clinical Response. You Are Not Failing. You Are Problem-Solving.
🔴 Child refuses to touch sensory bin or putty entirely
Clinical Response: Begin with watching only. Parent plays with material in child's presence. Week 1 goal: child is in the same room. Week 2: within arm's reach. Week 3: finger touch for 1 second. Never force hand contact — desensitisation requires child-led progression.
🔴 Sessions consistently shorter than 5 minutes
Clinical Response: Often a motivation issue, not a skill issue. Review reinforcement schedule (Card 18). Does the child's preferred reinforcer follow OT activity? Start with highest-preference material and work backwards.
🔴 Child uses all materials incorrectly (throws, bangs, mouths)
Clinical Response: Explore, not error. All early interaction with novel materials is valid. If mouthing is a safety concern: remove small objects and replace with large-only materials. Banging = proprioceptive seeking — try firmer materials.
🔴 Child cries during or after sessions consistently
Clinical Response: Stop immediately. Reassess readiness (Card 13). The intervention is too demanding or the session is too long. Reduce to one material, two minutes, zero demand. Consult OT immediately if distress persists across 3+ sessions.
🔴 Child performs well at clinic but resists home sessions
Clinical Response: Ask OT for a brief video of the exact clinic technique. Replicate the clinic setup as closely as possible. Have OT speak to child on a call before the first home session. The bridge gap is real and clinical.
🔴 No visible progress after 4 weeks
Clinical Response: Check session frequency first — partial implementation (2–3 times/week) reduces outcomes by ~60%. Review material difficulty — may need to step back one level. Contact Pinnacle OT for programme review: 9100 181 181.
🔴 Parent fatigue and session burnout
Clinical Response: This is universal and clinical. You are not alone. Rotate primary caregiver when possible. Reduce to 3 materials from 9. Accept a 7-minute session as a complete win. Consider joining the Pinnacle Parent Community (Card 32).
ACT III · CARD 22 · ADAPT AND PERSONALISE
No Two Children Are the Same. This Programme Is Not One-Size-Fits-All.
👆 Easier (Reduce Demand)
  • Use only 2 materials per session; reduce duration to 7 minutes
  • Remove all timed elements — follow child's rhythm
  • Increase reinforcement frequency to every 30 seconds
  • Parent does activity alongside child (parallel play)
✅ Standard
  • 3–5 materials per session; 17-minute template
  • Visual timer and schedule; reinforcement every completed activity
👇 Harder (Increase Challenge)
  • All 9 materials in one extended 25-minute session
  • Add cognitive demand: counting, naming, sorting by colour
  • Reduce parent support — child sets up own materials
  • Time trials: "How many pegs in 1 minute?"
Tactile Avoider (Hypersensitive)
Begin all sensory work with tools first. Sensory bin: start with dry rice only → kinetic sand weeks later. Putty: try through a plastic bag. Use gloves if needed — access is the goal, not bare-hand purity.
Sensory Seeker (Hyposensitive)
Add resistance to all materials (firmer putty, more textured bin fillings). Allow longer sensory bin time. Use balance board throughout session. Combine: put pom-poms inside sensory bin for tweezers-in-bin challenge.
ADHD Profile
Shorter rotations: 2 minutes per material maximum. Visual schedule is non-negotiable. Physical transition between materials: stand up, walk to next station. Build in 1-minute movement breaks.
Low Arousal Profile
Begin session with alerting input: jumping jacks, clapping, cold water on hands. Use bright colours and high-contrast materials. Enthusiastic, animated parent narration throughout. Upbeat music during active tasks.

Age-Specific: Ages 2–3: large pegs, large pom-poms, spring tweezers, soft putty only. Sessions 5–8 min. | Ages 4–6: all 9 materials, sessions 10–15 min. | Ages 7–10: full programme with cognitive complexity, sessions 15–20 min, generalisation to school tasks.

ACT IV · CARD 24 · WEEK 3–4
Week 3–4: The Neural Pathways Are Forming.
Watch for these consolidation signs — they are signals that the somatosensory cortex has adapted, the amygdala has formed a positive association, and the programme is working precisely as intended.
Anticipation
Child walks toward the materials area without being called. Asks about OT time. The association between the activity and positive outcome is forming in the amygdala — a profound neurological shift.
Preference Emergence
"Putty first!" This is the nervous system identifying which input meets its regulatory needs — a sophisticated, automatic calibration that was impossible in weeks 1–2.
Reduced Resistance
The sensory material that caused crying in week 1 is approached willingly in week 3. Tactile defensiveness thresholds shift with repeated structured exposure.
Generalisation Seeds
Child picks up objects with a pincer grip at meals. Holds a crayon differently. These are the first signs of skill transfer from OT material to real world — happening without instruction.
If your child is showing all 4 consolidation indicators by week 4: increase to harder difficulty (Card 22 slider) or add a fourth material to sessions. Do not rush progression — wait for clear signals.

Neuroplasticity evidence: Consolidation phase (weeks 3–4) represents critical period for pathway stabilisation. DOI:10.3389/fnint.2020.556660. You may also notice you're more confident — children read caregiver confidence and it directly affects their engagement.

ACT IV · CARD 27 · RED FLAGS
Your Child's Safety Is the Non-Negotiable Priority. Know When to Escalate.
🚩 Red Flag 1: Increasing Sensory Distress
Child's response to materials is becoming MORE distressed after 3+ weeks. Crying is increasing, avoidance is intensifying. This means the programme needs clinical recalibration — the current protocol is not matched to the child's sensory threshold.
🚩 Red Flag 2: Pain Responses
Child indicates pain (not discomfort) during activities. Any wincing, protective withdrawal, or verbalising "hurt" during OT activities requires immediate OT consultation. Material resistance grade may be inappropriate.
🚩 Red Flag 3: Balance Board Falls or Near-Falls
Multiple balance losses despite adult support. Programme must stop until OT re-assesses postural stability baseline. Do not continue balance board without OT clearance after a fall.
🚩 Red Flag 4: Skill Regression
Child was performing at a certain level and has now regressed significantly without explanation. Regression can signal illness, neurological change, medication adjustment, or significant environmental stressor. Document and report immediately.
🚩 Red Flag 5: Persistent Aggression During Sessions
If sessions consistently trigger aggressive behaviour (not refusal — aggression), this is a clinical signal requiring ABA and OT joint assessment. Do not continue programme without a support plan.

ACT VI · CARD 38 · FAQ
Questions Parents Ask Most. Answered by the Pinnacle OT Consortium.
Do I need a doctor's prescription to start this programme?
No prescription is needed to purchase any of the 9 materials or to follow F-619 as a general developmental support programme. However, if your child has a formal diagnosis (autism, developmental delay, cerebral palsy), a certified OT assessment makes outcomes significantly better. Call 9100 181 181 for a free consultation.
My child is 9 years old. Is it too late?
Absolutely not. The brain retains neuroplasticity throughout childhood and into adulthood. Fine motor skills can be built at any age with structured practice. Many children aged 8–12 show dramatic improvements with the F-619 programme. Start today.
How long before I see results?
Week 1–2 = tolerance building. Week 3–4 = visible behavioural changes. Week 5–8 = skill mastery and generalisation. Most parents report their first visible moment of progress between days 10–18. Keep the daily tracker (Card 20) — it helps you see gradual progress day-to-day.
My child refuses the therapy putty. Should I buy a different one?
Before purchasing anything: try the chapati dough DIY version first (Card 10) — its familiar smell reduces novelty-aversion. If resistance persists: use the indirect exposure approach — you play with the putty in the child's presence without any expectation. Never force contact. This is a clinical protocol, not a discipline issue.
Can we do all 9 materials in one session from the start?
Not initially. The 17-minute template uses 3–4 materials per session. As tolerance and skill increase over weeks 3–4, you can add more. Some children by week 8 can rotate through 6–7 materials in 20 minutes. Follow the child's pace — duration and breadth expand with capability, not parent ambition.
Our clinic OT uses different materials. Is F-619 still relevant?
Yes. F-619 is designed as a home complement to clinic-based OT, not a replacement. The 9 materials represent the most effective and accessible home-appropriate materials validated across our 20M+ session database. Your Pinnacle OT can advise on adjustments to align the home programme with your child's specific clinic protocol.
My child does the bin but refuses everything else. What do I do?
The sensory bin is your entry point — this is fine. Build the session routine and positive association through the bin for 2 weeks. Then: after 5 minutes of bin play, present tweezers beside the bin. "Let's use these to find objects in the bin." You have combined two materials using the bin as the motivator. This is the ABA pairing principle integrated with OT material sequencing.
Can I run sessions with my child's sibling present?
Cautiously, yes. For the first 2 weeks: solo sessions recommended. From week 3: if your child performs better with sibling present, this is perfectly acceptable clinically. If sibling wants to participate: give them their own set of materials. Never let a sibling take or interfere with the child's therapeutic materials during a session.
